subtitle: Lesson 3 · Noise Models in Quantum Systems

eyebrow: Spread a fixed error budget evenly

steps.label: Any single-qubit error reduces to I, X, Y, or Z
The depolarizing channel assigns one total error rate p
steps.sub: Then splits it evenly across the three non-trivial error types

steps.label: P(I) = 1 − p
steps.sub: Nothing happens to the qubit with probability 1 − p

steps.label: P(X) = P(Y) = P(Z) = p / 3
steps.sub: If something does happen, each error type is equally likely

eyebrow: The p/3 split at three illustrative error rates
caption: Whatever the total error budget p is, exactly a third of it goes to each of the three Pauli errors.

steps.label: The channel looks identical in any measurement basis
steps.sub: Same P(I)=1−p, P(X)=P(Y)=P(Z)=p/3 structure, whichever basis you pick

steps.label: That's why it's the model of choice for threshold estimates
steps.sub: The calculations that ask: below what error rate do more qubits help?

steps.label: It doesn't secretly favor bit-flips or phase-flips
steps.sub: So a threshold computed against it isn't tuned to flatter one code

steps.label: Not a claim that real hardware noise is this symmetric
steps.sub: Real qubits often show biased noise — more on that next

steps.label: Real superconducting and trapped-ion qubits show biased noise
steps.sub: Dephasing (Z-like) is often more frequent than relaxation-driven bit-flips

steps.label: That's because T2 is often shorter than T1 in practice
steps.sub: Lesson 1's two decoherence clocks don't run at equal rates

steps.label: Some advanced research deliberately exploits that asymmetry
steps.sub: Biased-noise codes, rather than assuming the symmetric picture

steps.label: For this course: the standard yardstick quoted in papers
steps.sub: Useful and widely used — explicitly not the full physical picture
